title: Containerization with Docker

# Containerization with Docker ##### "But it works on my machine" A student finished a plant-disease classifier and sent the repository to a friend for testing. What followed was three days of messages. The friend had Python 3.9; the project needed 3.11. Then a package failed to build because a C compiler was missing. Then TensorFlow installed but crashed, because the friend was on an Apple Silicon Mac and the pinned version was x86-only. Then it ran but produced different predictions — a transitive dependency had resolved to a newer version with changed default behaviour. The model was fine. The **environment** was the problem, and environments are invisible until they break. Docker eliminates this. You package the application *and its entire environment* — the operating system libraries, the Python version, every dependency at an exact version — into an image that runs identically anywhere Docker runs. The friend's three days become one command. ##### Containers versus virtual machines Both provide isolation; they differ in what they virtualize, and that difference is the whole story. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph VM["Virtual machines"] direction TB V1[App A] --- V2[App B] V1 --- G1[Guest OS
~2 GB each] V2 --- G2[Guest OS
~2 GB each] G1 --- HY[Hypervisor] G2 --- HY HY --- HOS1[Host OS] HOS1 --- HW1[Hardware] end subgraph CON["Containers"] direction TB C1[App A] --- C2[App B] C1 --- D[Docker Engine] C2 --- D D --- HOS2[Host OS — shared kernel] HOS2 --- HW2[Hardware] end ``` A **virtual machine** virtualizes hardware and runs a complete guest operating system with its own kernel. Strong isolation, and a heavy price: gigabytes of disk, hundreds of megabytes of RAM per VM, and boot times measured in tens of seconds. A **container** virtualizes only the operating system's user space, **sharing the host kernel**. Isolation comes from Linux primitives — namespaces for what a process can see, cgroups for what it can use. The result is megabytes rather than gigabytes, and startup in under a second. | | Virtual machine | Container | |---|---|---| | Virtualizes | Hardware | Operating system | | Kernel | Own guest kernel | **Shared with host** | | Size | GB | MB | | Startup | 30–60 seconds | **< 1 second** | | Density per host | Tens | Hundreds | | Isolation strength | **Stronger** | Good (shared kernel) | That kernel sharing is why containers are lightweight and also why their isolation is weaker — a kernel vulnerability affects every container on the host, whereas VMs remain separated. For ML workloads the trade is almost always worth it, and container overhead versus running natively is close to negligible. **Reproducibility** comes from a different property: an image is an immutable, layered filesystem snapshot. The same image bytes produce the same environment on your laptop, your colleague's Mac and a cloud server. ##### Writing a Dockerfile A Dockerfile is a recipe. Each instruction creates a **layer**, and layers are cached — which is the single most important fact for writing good ones. ```dockerfile # ---------- Stage 1: build dependencies ---------- FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \ PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 \ PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1 # Build tools live only in this stage RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \ build-essential gcc \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* WORKDIR /app # Dependencies FIRST — this layer is cached until requirements.txt changes COPY requirements.txt . RUN python -m venv /opt/venv \ && /opt/venv/bin/pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt # ---------- Stage 2: runtime ---------- FROM python:3.11-slim AS runtime ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \ PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH" RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* \ && useradd --create-home --uid 10001 appuser COPY --from=builder /opt/venv /opt/venv WORKDIR /app COPY --chown=appuser:appuser ./models ./models COPY --chown=appuser:appuser ./src ./src # source LAST — changes most often USER appuser # never run as root EXPOSE 8000 HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=30s --retries=3 \ CMD curl -fsS http://localhost:8000/health/ready || exit 1 CMD ["uvicorn", "src.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"] ``` Five decisions in that file matter, and together they are the difference between a 1.9 GB image that rebuilds in four minutes and a 400 MB one that rebuilds in twenty seconds. **Order least-changing first.** The `COPY requirements.txt` / `pip install` pair is cached until dependencies change, so editing a line of source code rebuilds only the final layers. Copying source before installing dependencies invalidates the cache on every commit — the most common and most costly Dockerfile mistake. **Multi-stage build.** `build-essential` and `gcc` are needed to compile wheels but not to run them. Stage two copies only the finished virtualenv, leaving several hundred megabytes of toolchain behind. **Slim base image.** `python:3.11-slim` is roughly 150 MB against `python:3.11`'s ~1 GB. Alpine is smaller still but uses musl libc, which breaks many scientific Python wheels — slim is the right default for ML. **Non-root user** with a numeric UID. A container escape as root is a materially worse incident, and Kubernetes' `runAsNonRoot` requires a numeric ID. **`PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1`** ensures logs appear immediately rather than sitting in a buffer, which matters enormously when debugging a container. Add a `.dockerignore`, or `COPY` will drag in your `.git` directory, virtual environment and datasets: ```text .git .venv __pycache__/ *.pyc .env data/ notebooks/ tests/ *.ipynb ``` For ML projects that last entry matters: **`data/` in `.dockerignore`** prevents accidentally baking a 2 GB dataset into your image. ##### Building and running ```bash docker build -t fraud-api:1.0.0 . docker images fraud-api # check the size docker run -d --name fraud-api \ -p 8000:8000 \ --env-file .env \ --memory=2g --cpus=2 \ --restart unless-stopped \ fraud-api:1.0.0 docker logs -f fraud-api docker exec -it fraud-api bash # shell inside the running container docker stats fraud-api # live resource usage docker stop fraud-api && docker rm fraud-api ``` Three operational notes. **Tag with a version**, never rely on `latest` — you cannot roll back to a tag that keeps moving. **Pass secrets via `--env-file`**, never bake them into the image, because they persist in the layer history and travel with every copy. And **set resource limits**, or one container can starve the host. ##### Handling ML-specific concerns **Model files** present a genuine choice. Baking them into the image makes it self-contained and immutable — good for reproducibility, but a 2 GB model means a 2 GB image pushed and pulled on every deploy. Mounting them at runtime keeps images small but adds a dependency on external storage. The practical rule: **bake models under ~200 MB, mount or download larger ones at startup.** **GPU access** requires the NVIDIA Container Toolkit and a CUDA base image: ```dockerfile FROM nvidia/cuda:12.1.0-runtime-ubuntu22.04 RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3.11 python3-pip # ... rest as before ``` ```bash docker run --gpus all -p 8000:8000 fraud-api:1.0.0-gpu ``` Note that GPU images are large — several gigabytes — because CUDA runtime libraries are substantial. Use a CPU image unless you genuinely need GPU inference. **Dependency pinning** is more important in ML than in most software, because numerical libraries change behaviour between versions: ```text # requirements.txt — pin exact versions fastapi==0.115.0 uvicorn[standard]==0.32.0 scikit-learn==1.5.2 pandas==2.2.3 numpy==2.1.2 ``` `scikit-learn>=1.5` will one day resolve to 2.0 and your pickled model may fail to load. Generate the file with `pip freeze > requirements.txt` and commit it. ##### Docker Compose Compose describes multi-container applications in one file — the model API, the Streamlit UI, a database, all started together. ```yaml services: api: build: context: . dockerfile: Dockerfile target: runtime image: fraud-api:1.0.0 environment: MODEL_PATH: /app/models/fraud_v1.joblib LOG_LEVEL: info env_file: [.env] volumes: - ./models:/app/models:ro # read-only mount healthcheck: test: ["CMD", "curl", "-fsS", "http://localhost:8000/health/ready"] interval: 30s start_period: 40s retries: 3 deploy: resources: limits: { memory: 2g, cpus: "2" } logging: driver: json-file options: { max-size: "10m", max-file: "3" } networks: [backend] restart: unless-stopped ui: build: context: ./ui ports: ["8501:8501"] environment: API_URL: http://api:8000 # service NAME, not localhost depends_on: api: condition: service_healthy # wait for readiness, not just start networks: [backend] restart: unless-stopped networks: backend: ``` ```bash docker compose up -d --build docker compose ps docker compose logs -f api docker compose down # stop; named volumes survive ``` Two details prevent common failures. **`API_URL: http://api:8000`** uses the service name — inside a Compose network, `localhost` refers to the container itself, not to sibling services, and this catches everyone once. And **`condition: service_healthy`** waits for the healthcheck to pass rather than merely for the container to start, which prevents the UI crash-looping while the model loads. Add **log rotation** as shown; an unbounded `json-file` driver will eventually fill the host disk. ##### Common mistakes - **`COPY . .` before installing dependencies**, destroying the layer cache. - **No `.dockerignore`**, shipping `.git`, `.venv` and datasets into the image. - **Running as root.** - **Unpinned dependency versions**, so builds are not reproducible over time. - **Secrets baked into the image** via `ENV` or `ARG` — they persist in layer history. - **`latest` tags**, making rollback impossible. - **`localhost` between Compose services** instead of the service name. - **`depends_on` without a health condition**, causing startup races. - **Baking multi-gigabyte models** into images. - **No `PYTHONUNBUFFERED`**, so logs appear late or not at all. - **No resource limits**, letting one container destabilize the host. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: write a **Dockerfile for your FastAPI model service**, build the image, and run the container serving predictions locally. Then do the instructive experiment — build once, change a single line of source, and rebuild. If it takes four minutes, your dependency install is after your source copy; fix the ordering and watch it drop to seconds. The mini project is a **full ML app containerized with Docker Compose** — model API plus a Streamlit UI — starting with one command. Then test the actual claim: send the repository to someone else and see whether `docker compose up` works on their machine. That is the three-days-of-messages problem, solved or not solved, and it is the only real proof. For the assignment, **explain the difference between a container and a VM and why containers are lightweight and reproducible**. Cover the mechanism rather than the summary: VMs virtualize hardware and run a full guest kernel, while containers share the host kernel and isolate via namespaces and cgroups — which is why one is gigabytes and slow to boot while the other is megabytes and near-instant. For reproducibility, explain that an image is an immutable layered filesystem containing the exact OS libraries, language runtime and pinned dependencies, so the same bytes produce the same environment everywhere. Mention the trade-off honestly: shared kernel means weaker isolation than a VM. ##### Key takeaways - Containers share the host kernel and isolate with namespaces and cgroups, making them megabytes and sub-second rather than gigabytes and slow like VMs. - Order Dockerfile instructions least-changing first — dependencies before source — or every code edit triggers a full rebuild. - Use multi-stage builds and slim base images to leave build toolchains behind, and always run as a non-root numeric UID. - Pin exact dependency versions and keep datasets and secrets out of images; bake small models, mount or download large ones. - Compose describes the whole stack in one file — use service names for inter-container URLs and `condition: service_healthy` to avoid startup races.
